newsitem.title: CANADA: CanOxy chief expects victory in Wascana battle.
newsitem.headline: CanOxy chief expects victory in Wascana battle.

text.p: The chief executive of Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd., whose stock has jumped since the company's C$2 billion ($1.45 billion) white knight bid for Wascana Energy Inc., said on Tuesday he was confident of winning the takeover battle.

In what would be the richest merger in Canada's oil patch in three years, CanOxy last week unveiled a C$20.50 ($14.97) a share cash bid for Wascana, which eclipsed a hostile cash and stock offer from rival Talisman Energy Inc..

"We basically did a stretch to get there and I think it's certainly a full-value price," CanOxy's David Hentschel told Reuters in an interview after meetings in eastern Canada with the company's major shareholders.
"We're confident that will be borne out over the next 21 days as we acquire stock through the tender process."
If CanOxy wins, its production is expected to grow to 264,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 1997, including 115,000 in Canada, placing it among the country's top three producers.

Hentschel said playing white knight for Regina, Saskatchewan-based Wascana, a former government-owned energy company known for its heavy crude oil production, gave CanOxy a strong advantage over Talisman.

Before jumping into the fray, Calgary-based CanOxy, 30 percent-owned by Occidental Petroleum Corp. of Los Angeles, was rumored as a potential bidder because many Wascana exploration and production lands in Saskatchewan overlapped its own.
CanOxy was also in the market for a source of steady cash flow to balance several global high-risk exploration plays.
But the company waited until an unsolicited bid was made for Wascana before making its move.
"There are certain disadvantages in being a hostile bidder as evidenced by this particular exercise," said Hentschel, a 63-year-old Kansas-born and Louisiana-raised career oilman.
He said a big drawback for a hostile bidder was not gaining access to Wascana's confidential financial and operating data, something for which Talisman lobbied to no avail.

Talisman Chief Executive Jim Buckee has said his company could increase its bid, but only if it was sure of higher value. Talisman, which extended its bid on Monday, has offered C$18.50 ($13.50) cash or 0.41 of a Talisman share for each Wascana share.

Hentschel said the odds were slim of a third bidder surfacing before CanOxy's bid expired on April 14 because of an extensive process by Wascana and its financial advisers in seeking alternatives after Talisman launched its advance.
CanOxy's post-deal debt level of C$2.5 billion ($1.8 billion) or 2.5 times its projected annual cash flow, has raised investor concern.

But Hentschel said he believed the company's debt payment record would calm any fears. CanOxy's debt was five times cash flow in the early stages of its huge development in Yemen, its most famous producing area.

CanOxy shares were off C50 cents to C$26.50 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday. The stock has climbed from C$23.50 the day before it launched its offer. Wascana was up C5 cents to C$20.65 in Toronto, while Talisman fell C25 cents to C$43.
